passages.text: The image of the corporation as an instrument for maximising returns to its owners — the so-called shareholder primacy model — has dominated business education for half a century. A more recent strand of research, drawing on the experience of around eight thousand firms in roughly ninety countries, has revisited the question of whether companies can credibly pursue a wider set of obligations and remain commercially viable. The institutional vehicle most often examined is the certified B-Corporation, a designation introduced in 2007 by a non-profit body in the United States and now adopted in dozens of jurisdictions. The story matters because the answer shapes how regulators, investors and managers think about the legitimate purpose of the firm.

Three broad positions dominate the current literature. The first, defended by Professor Marta Velasco of IESE Business School in Barcelona, argues that legally embedding a duty to consider workers, suppliers, communities and the environment, alongside shareholders, produces measurable improvements in employee retention and supplier relations without significant losses on conventional financial measures. Velasco's 2022 analysis of two thousand and forty matched pairs of European firms reported a roughly twelve per cent lower voluntary-turnover rate at certified B-Corps over a five-year window, with no statistically significant gap in return on assets. The second position, associated with Dr Soren Yamashita of the University of Tokyo, emphasises the limits of voluntary certification. Yamashita's group has documented that certified firms are disproportionately concentrated in consumer-facing sectors where reputational gains are most visible, and notes that the model has spread less readily into heavy industry, where the financial stakes of any commitment are larger.

A third position is offered by Professor Adaeze Okonkwo, an economic sociologist at the London School of Economics. Okonkwo accepts the descriptive findings of both her colleagues but argues that the more interesting question is institutional. In a 2023 mixed-methods study covering one hundred and twelve firms across four jurisdictions, her team traced how stakeholder commitments survive changes of ownership and senior management. The pattern, she suggests, depends less on certification itself than on whether the underlying obligations are written into the company's articles of association in a form that subsequent boards cannot easily dilute. Where such legal anchoring is in place, the obligations tend to persist; where the commitment relies on culture alone, it tends to erode within roughly a decade.

Not all researchers accept the optimistic readings. Critics, including Dr Henrik Lindqvist of the Stockholm School of Economics, have argued that many published B-Corp studies have struggled to separate the effect of certification from the prior characteristics of firms that choose to certify. Lindqvist's group reviewed forty-seven empirical papers and found that around two-thirds did not adequately control for self-selection. He does not deny that the model can work, but insists that the headline figures often reported in the financial press should be treated as a ceiling on the true effect, rather than as an unbiased estimate of it.

What the four accounts share, despite their differences, is a preference for treating stakeholder governance as a question of design rather than slogan. Velasco's matched-pairs evidence works best when paired with Okonkwo's emphasis on legal anchoring. Yamashita's sectoral concentration findings work best when paired with Lindqvist's caution about self-selection. The most carefully designed studies, the literature suggests, treat certification as one element of a broader institutional package, even though commercial pressures often push firms to claim a single, marketable identity.

Some implications for policy follow. Several European jurisdictions have begun to introduce optional legal forms that allow companies to embed stakeholder obligations directly into their constitutions, including the Societa Benefit in Italy from 2016 and the Entreprise a Mission in France from 2019. Early evaluations from both regimes suggest moderate take-up by mid-sized firms and limited engagement so far from listed multinationals, where shareholder pressure remains strong. Whether these legal forms will outgrow their current niche or remain a minority option depends, in Okonkwo's view, on whether institutional investors begin to treat them as a credible signal rather than as a marketing exercise.

This is not to suggest that stakeholder governance is settled doctrine. The evidence base is uneven across regions, the sample of firms that certify remains skewed, and the longer-term effects on innovation and capital allocation remain a matter of debate. The aim of the more thoughtful research, the literature suggests, is not to declare the shareholder model obsolete but to identify the conditions under which a wider conception of corporate purpose can be credibly maintained without forcing the firms that adopt it into commercial disadvantage.

A further point of contention concerns measurement. Several research teams have noted that the conventional financial indicators on which comparison studies depend — return on assets, voluntary-turnover rates, share-price performance — capture only a narrow slice of the outcomes that stakeholder governance is supposed to influence. Indicators of supplier resilience, community engagement and environmental performance are, by most accounts, less standardised and less comparable across jurisdictions, which complicates any clean test of the model. Until the measurement question is more settled, headline figures will probably remain contested even when the underlying data are themselves accepted as broadly accurate.

audio_scripts.text: Good morning. Today's lecture continues our corporate-responsibility research strand, focusing on the empirical literature around B-Corporation certification — the so-called "B-Corp" movement — and what we now know about its measurable effects on firm behaviour. [pause:5s] The conceptual scaffolding I'll draw on is taken from the work of Professor Esperanza Mbongwe-Cruz — that's M-B-O-N-G-W-E hyphen C-R-U-Z; one hyphen between Mbongwe and Cruz, and the M and B are pronounced as a single voiced cluster. So Mbongwe-Cruz. Her 2018 monograph reframed CSR analysis from a one-dimensional reputational lens into what she calls "stakeholder-impact accounting". [pause:3s] Right. A brief tense-orientation note. Mbongwe-Cruz's framework USED TO be evaluated through reputational-survey instruments only, NOW the field deploys triangulated mixed-methods designs incorporating audited disclosures, supply-chain telemetry, and worker-voice transcripts, and from 2029 a multi-jurisdiction consortium WILL be rolling out blockchain-verified impact modules. Past, present, future. For today's purposes I'm focusing on the CURRENT methodological state — that is, audited mixed-methods. [pause:3s] The longitudinal cohort I want to reference today was first surveyed in 2017 — sorry, let me correct that, 2016; the published descriptive statistics in 2017 covered baseline data collected in 2016. So whenever I refer to the baseline year for the certified-firm cohort, please record 2016. [pause:3s] Moving to terminology. The construct Mbongwe-Cruz foregrounds — a structured ledger of audited non-financial outcomes spanning workers, community, environment, and governance — is termed "stakeholder-impact accounting". You'll encounter related labels in the older literature: triple bottom line, social audit, sustainability reporting. All of these gesture toward overlapping phenomena, but they are NOT interchangeable with Mbongwe-Cruz's term. The currently accepted scholarly term is stakeholder-impact accounting — s-t-a-k-e-h-o-l-d-e-r hyphen impact accounting. So when the older literature uses triple bottom line or sustainability reporting, that's a related but distinct construct. [pause:3s] The next domain I want to discuss is what business ethicists call the "purpose-profit spectrum". When ethnographers describe how certified firms balance ethical commitments against margin pressure, they sketch a graded continuum running from purpose-primary through purpose-integrated to purpose-decorative. So, you know, you'll see firms whose B-Corp status genuinely shapes procurement — that's purpose-integrated. Or firms who, kinda, just slap a badge on the website — that's purpose-decorative. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the technical term itself. The umbrella term is the purpose-profit spectrum. [pause:3s] Now, the survey data — and this is where I want you to pay close attention, because the quantifiers cluster densely here. Of the five hundred and eighty certified firms we sampled across eleven sectors last year, MOST demonstrated measurable impact gains post-certification — roughly seventy-four per cent. Only a few — about eight per cent — showed a regression in audited outcomes, and some — eighteen per cent — reported flat or context-dependent trajectories. So measurable-gain dominates numerically, but the eight-per-cent regression tail, though small, is theoretically significant. [pause:3s] A second key construct I want to flag is "ethical drift". This refers to a temporal pattern in which certified firms gradually relax adherence to original commitments without losing certification — sometimes within a single recertification cycle. At the Rotterdam cohort site, our auditors documented one hundred and twelve drift episodes across the cohort during one three-year window. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that certification linearly improves all impact dimensions is, frankly, not supported. Most of the firms in our sample did NOT exhibit the predicted uniform improvement across all four impact dimensions. Quite the opposite — many showed asymmetric profiles, with governance scores climbing while environmental scores stagnated. So the older "halo certification" hypothesis, which predicts uniform uplift, is empirically NOT corroborated by our data. [pause:3s] Let me return to something I touched on earlier — the methodological tense-orientation point I made at the start. That CURRENT audited mixed-methods state is what we're, sorta, gonna scrutinise in tomorrow's seminar. I want you to focus on the worker-voice transcripts specifically, not the blockchain futures or the legacy reputational-survey instruments. [pause:3s] To summarise: B-Corp outcomes are best understood through stakeholder-impact accounting, not single-axis reputation; the technical term for the audited ledger of non-financial outcomes is stakeholder-impact accounting; measurable-gain dominates at roughly seventy-four per cent; and the halo-certification hypothesis is not empirically supported in this cohort. Next week we'll examine green-bond markets. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: Whether corporations exist solely to enrich their shareholders is one of the most contested questions in modern business ethics. While some commentators continue to defend shareholder primacy, I largely disagree with the view, because corporations operate within wider social and ecological systems whose health ultimately determines their own.

Supporters of the traditional model argue that a clear focus on returns disciplines management. It is the pressure to deliver quarterly results that, in their view, prevents executives from squandering funds on vanity projects. Moreover, profitable firms generate jobs, fund pensions and contribute taxes, all of which arguably benefit society far more than performative philanthropy. From this angle, prioritising shareholders is not selfish but efficient, since a thriving business is the precondition for almost every other social good a company might deliver.

However, this position increasingly seems out of step with how value is actually created today. Modern companies rely on stakeholders far beyond their investors - workers, suppliers, regulators and the communities hosting their factories. When firms cut corners to flatter the bottom line, the costs do not disappear; they are simply transferred to society as pollution, sweatshops or unsafe products. The 2008 financial crisis showed how the single-minded pursuit of returns can destroy the very economy on which those returns depend. The rise of ESG investing further suggests that even shareholders themselves now demand a broader scorecard.

In conclusion, I disagree strongly with the proposition that shareholder value should override everything else. A more balanced model, often described as stakeholder capitalism, would better protect long-term profitability while limiting social harm. What the corporate world needs is not a softer version of greed, but a genuinely broader definition of success.

Few doctrines have shaped contemporary capitalism as profoundly as Milton Friedman's claim that the social responsibility of business is to increase its profits. While the slogan retains rhetorical force, I disagree strongly with the proposition that shareholder value should override every other consideration, for it rests on an outdated reading of where corporate value actually originates.

Defenders of shareholder primacy do raise legitimate points. By anchoring management to a single, measurable objective, the doctrine arguably reduces agency costs and curbs executive self-dealing. Profitable corporations, in turn, finance pensions, generate tax revenue and discipline inefficient competitors out of the market. It is precisely this hard-edged accountability, proponents contend, that distinguishes private enterprise from politically captured state monopolies.

Yet this account understates the breadth of fiduciary duty in the twenty-first century. Modern firms depend on stakeholders whose contributions appear nowhere on the balance sheet: workers absorbing precarity, regulators granting licences and ecosystems supplying inputs. What shareholder maximisation has tended to produce, particularly in resource-intensive sectors, is a systematic transfer of risk onto these groups - wage suppression, sweatshop subcontracting and environmental externalities masked as efficiency. Were such costs internalised, many headline returns would evaporate overnight. Nowhere is this clearer than in the post-2008 banking sector, where shareholder-driven risk-taking demanded taxpayer bailouts worth trillions.

Furthermore, the trajectory of capital markets is itself shifting. The rapid mainstreaming of ESG criteria suggests that long-term investors increasingly penalise narrow profit-maximisation, while reputational shocks now translate swiftly into lost market value. What sustainable companies appear to grasp is that legitimacy, not merely earnings, secures the social licence to operate. On balance, then, shareholder value remains a useful metric, but elevating it above all else is intellectually obsolete and commercially imprudent; stakeholder capitalism, properly governed, is the more defensible model for our age.

Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. The billionaire engaged in philanthropy, donating millions of dollars to charity throughout his life. — PHILANTHROPY (n) = hoạt động từ thiện; collocation "corporate philanthropy", "engage in philanthropy", "genuine philanthropy".

2. The company holds a monopoly on this market, leaving customers with no real alternative. — MONOPOLY (n) = thế độc quyền; collocation "hold a monopoly", "monopoly on the market", "break up a monopoly".

3. Shareholders are demanding greater transparency about how the firm spends its money. — TRANSPARENCY (n) = tính minh bạch; collocation "financial transparency", "demand transparency", "improve transparency".

4. Before making major decisions, the board engages stakeholders, including employees, customers, and local communities. — STAKEHOLDERS (n) = các bên liên quan; collocation "engage stakeholders", "key stakeholders", "stakeholder interests".
5. The two banks announced a merger to become one larger organisation. — MERGER (n) = sự sáp nhập; collocation "announce a merger", "merger and acquisition", "pursue a strategic merger".

6. Critics accused the airline of greenwashing, falsely claiming to be environmentally friendly while doing little to reduce pollution. — GREENWASHING (n) = "tẩy xanh", giả vờ thân thiện môi trường; collocation "accuse of greenwashing", "greenwashing tactics", "prevent greenwashing".

7. The firm has grown into a huge conglomerate operating in many different industries. — CONGLOMERATE (n) = tập đoàn đa ngành; collocation "a multinational conglomerate", "a diversified conglomerate", "conglomerate structure".
8. The small business found success by carving out a niche rather than targeting the mass market. — NICHE (n) = thị trường ngách; collocation "niche market", "target a niche", "carve out a niche".

9. Investors are calling for greater corporate accountability when a company's products cause harm. — ACCOUNTABILITY (n) = trách nhiệm giải trình; collocation "corporate accountability", "hold accountable", "demand accountability".

10. Several employees reported allegations of malpractice within the finance department. — MALPRACTICE (n) = hành vi sai trái trong nghề nghiệp; collocation "corporate malpractice", "allegations of malpractice", "medical malpractice".

11. The factory has committed to using sustainable supply chains that do not damage the environment in the long term. — SUSTAINABLE (adj) = bền vững; collocation "sustainable supply chains", "environmentally sustainable", "sustainable growth".

12. Human rights groups have criticised some factories for the exploitation of their workers, including extremely low wages. — EXPLOITATION (n) = sự bóc lột; collocation "labour/worker exploitation", "exploitation of resources".
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu

1. Band 7: Large companies should pay higher taxes given the substantial profits they generate. Band 8: Given the substantial profits many multinationals generate, it seems only reasonable that they should be subject to significantly higher rates of corporate taxation.

2. Band 7: Many people believe that CEO pay has become excessive compared with what ordinary employees earn. Band 8: The widening gap between executive remuneration and average worker pay has led many to question whether current CEO salaries can still be justified on merit alone.

3. Band 7: Companies frequently claim to prioritise environmental responsibility, yet their actions do not always reflect this. Band 8: While many corporations profess a strong commitment to sustainability, such claims are often undermined by practices that amount to little more than greenwashing.

4. Band 7: Consumers are increasingly favouring businesses that treat their employees fairly. Band 8: A growing segment of consumers is gravitating towards businesses perceived to uphold fair labour practices, rewarding ethical conduct with brand loyalty.

5. Band 7: A company's reputation can suffer considerably if it is found to have acted dishonestly. Band 8: Should a company be exposed for dishonest practices, the resulting reputational damage can prove far more costly than any short-term financial gain.

6. Band 7: Small businesses often find it difficult to compete with large corporations that dominate the market. Band 8: Small enterprises frequently struggle to compete on equal terms with conglomerates that hold a near-monopoly over key segments of the market.

7. Band 7: Governments need to introduce clear regulations to prevent companies from causing environmental harm. Band 8: Robust regulatory frameworks are essential if governments are to hold corporations properly accountable for the environmental harm their operations may cause.

8. Band 7: Being honest with customers plays a vital role in building long-term trust. Band 8: Transparency in dealings with customers is fundamental to cultivating the kind of long-term trust on which brand loyalty ultimately depends.

blocks.text: 1. Facts & Trends (Dữ liệu thực tế để support cho bài Writing)

The Rise of ESG Investing: Investors are increasingly using Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) criteria to evaluate companies, punishing those with poor ethical records by withdrawing funding.
Tech Monopolies (Big Tech): A handful of massive corporations now dominate global digital advertising and e-commerce, raising concerns about data privacy and the crushing of smaller competitors.
Supply Chain Scrutiny: Consumers can now trace product origins using blockchain technology, making it impossible for brands to hide their reliance on sweatshops or unethical raw material sourcing.
2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: Profit vs. Social Responsibility

Profit-First View: A business's sole obligation is to survive, provide jobs, and generate returns for shareholders; imposing costly CSR initiatives can lead to bankruptcy, resulting in massive unemployment.

Social Responsibility View: Corporations utilise public infrastructure and natural resources, therefore they owe a debt to society; ethical behaviour (avoiding exploitation, philanthropy) actively builds a strong brand image, which ultimately drives long-term revenue.
Topic: Government Bailouts of Failing Businesses

Arguments FOR Bailouts: Prevents catastrophic rises in unemployment during a recession; protects vital national industries (like aviation or banking) that are "too big to fail" without triggering a severe economic collapse.

Arguments AGAINST Bailouts: Encourages reckless financial behaviour by executives (moral hazard); wastes taxpayer money to reward incompetent management; naturally failing companies should be allowed to go bust to make room for more efficient competitors.
Topic: Salary Caps for High-level Executives

Arguments FOR Caps: Reduces extreme wealth inequality within companies; redirects funds towards improving working conditions and the remuneration of low-level employees; prevents executives from taking excessive short-term risks to inflate their own bonuses.

Arguments AGAINST Caps: Top-tier talent will simply migrate to countries or industries without caps (brain drain); running a massive multinational conglomerate involves immense liability and pressure, justifying astronomical pay.

Model Answer (Band 7.5-8.0, ~270 words)

The company I'd like to talk about is Vinamilk, Vietnam's largest dairy producer, which — beyond its commercial dominance — has, in my opinion, demonstrably reshaped public health and rural livelihoods over the past four decades. Founded in 1976 as a state-owned enterprise, it has since transformed into a publicly listed conglomerate with a market capitalisation exceeding 150 trillion VND.

What Vinamilk does, fundamentally, is produce dairy products — from liquid milk and yoghurt to infant formula — but the more interesting story lies in its broader operational footprint. The company sources from over 130,000 smallholder farmers, runs 15 organic farms, and exports to more than 60 countries, including stringently regulated markets like Japan and the UAE.

The societal impact, I'd argue, manifests in three concrete ways. Firstly, the company spearheaded the National School Milk Programme, which has provided subsidised dairy to roughly 3.3 million primary schoolchildren since 2016, measurably improving nutritional outcomes in provinces where stunting rates had remained stubbornly high. Secondly, what Vinamilk has done is professionalise smallholder dairy farming by providing veterinary support, guaranteed pricing, and technical training — effectively pulling thousands of rural households out of subsistence agriculture. Thirdly, the firm's commitment to transparency in its supply chain, audited by independent third parties, sets a benchmark that few domestic competitors can match.

Were it not for sustained CSR investment of this scale, the dairy sector here would likely still be dominated by imported powdered formula. All in all, Vinamilk strikes me as a rare instance where shareholder returns and stakeholder welfare have been genuinely aligned, rather than the former being prioritised at the latter's expense — a model worth replicating across other industries.

blocks.text: Q1: Should corporations be taxed more?

Point: I'd argue that effective corporate tax rates, particularly on multinationals, are currently far too low and ought to be raised — though the mechanism matters enormously, and blunt rate hikes alone tend to backfire.

Explain: The fundamental problem is that decades of tax competition between jurisdictions have allowed conglomerates to engage in sophisticated profit-shifting, parking earnings in low-tax havens while extracting value from high-tax markets. This erodes the fiscal base that funds public goods like education and healthcare, which those same corporations rely upon for their workforce.

Example: The OECD's Pillar Two agreement, signed by 138 countries in 2021, finally established a 15% global minimum corporate tax — a long-overdue measure projected to recover roughly $220 billion in annual revenue. Apple's notorious arrangement in Ireland, where it paid an effective rate of just 0.005% in 2014, illustrates precisely the kind of fiduciary acrobatics that the new framework targets.
Link: So rather than crude rate increases, what's needed is coordinated international enforcement — and the OECD deal, while imperfect, is a meaningful step in the right direction.
Q2: Are CEO salaries justified?

Point: Frankly, the prevailing CEO pay structures in many Western economies have, in my view, become indefensible — though I'd stop short of arguing that all executive compensation is inherently unjustified.

Explain: The core issue is the staggering disparity: in 1965, US CEOs earned roughly 20 times the typical worker; by 2022, that ratio had ballooned to 344-to-1, according to the Economic Policy Institute. Much of this windfall is tied to short-term share-price performance, which incentivises buybacks and cost-cutting rather than genuine value creation.

Example: Take the 2008 financial crisis, where executives at Lehman Brothers and Bear Stearns walked away with nine-figure payouts despite presiding over institutional collapse — a textbook case of moral hazard. By contrast, Japanese firms maintain a CEO-to-worker ratio of around 11-to-1, with no discernible loss of competitiveness, which rather punctures the "talent flight" justification.

Link: What this suggests is that astronomical pay reflects governance failures and captured boards more than genuine market efficiency — and incremental caps tied to median worker pay would be a sensible corrective.
Q3: Can capitalism be sustainable?

Point: Capitalism, I would tentatively suggest, can be made compatible with sustainability — but only through substantial structural reform, not the cosmetic greenwashing that currently passes for corporate responsibility.

Explain: The fundamental tension is that conventional capitalism externalises environmental costs onto third parties and future generations, treating ecosystems as free inputs rather than finite capital. Sustainability requires internalising those costs through carbon pricing, regulation, and stakeholder governance — none of which dilute markets but rather correct their blind spots.

Example: Patagonia's recent move to transfer ownership to a climate-focused trust, with profits funnelled into environmental causes, represents one credible model — albeit a niche one. More systemically, the EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, in force since 2024, now mandates that roughly 50,000 firms disclose ESG metrics, making greenwashing legally hazardous. Conversely, the 2023 collapse of carbon offset markets exposed how much "sustainable capitalism" remains performative.
Link: So while reformed capitalism is plausible, the window is narrow — and absent serious regulatory teeth, voluntary corporate goodwill simply won't move the needle fast enough.

4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Welcome back. Today I want to interrogate the architecture of contemporary corporate accountability through three lenses: stakeholder theory, corporate governance and ESG metrics. The boardroom orthodoxy of the late twentieth century, I will argue, is now intellectually bankrupt.

> Let us begin with stakeholder theory, articulated most influentially by the philosopher R. Edward Freeman in 1984. Freeman contended that a corporation owes obligations not solely to its shareholders, but to a constellation of constituencies — employees, suppliers, host communities and the natural environment. The doctrine displaces the famous Milton Friedman dictum that "the social responsibility of business is to increase its profits". The pendulum, demonstrably, has swung.

> Now, corporate governance. The Enron collapse of 2001 exposed how opaque accounting, interlocking directorates and a compliant audit firm — Arthur Andersen — could mask systemic malfeasance until the very moment of liquidation. The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 imposed stricter disclosure regimes, but governance failures recur: Wirecard, Theranos, FTX. The recurring fault line is the fiduciary duty of independent directors, which is too often honoured in rhetoric and breached in practice.

> Finally, ESG metrics. By 2023, assets governed by environmental, social and governance criteria had surpassed thirty trillion US dollars globally. Yet the proliferation of competing rating agencies — MSCI, Sustainalytics, ISS — has produced a phenomenon researchers term aggregate confusion: the same firm can be ranked top quartile by one provider and bottom quartile by another. Worse, greenwashing has become endemic, with marketing departments outpacing substantive reform.

Now, table three will quantify some of this, but first let me complicate the rather tidy picture I have painted — because there is a structural objection to stakeholder theory that its critics press hard, and I think we should meet it head-on. The objection runs like this: when a director is accountable to everyone, she is in practice accountable to no one. Michael Jensen made this argument sharply — he called it the problem of a single objective function. If you instruct managers to balance the interests of shareholders, employees, communities and the planet simultaneously, you give them no clear yardstick, and, well, an unmeasurable mandate becomes an unaccountable one. [pause] Managerial discretion expands, and self-serving behaviour hides behind the language of virtue.

That is not a knockout blow, but it sharpens what good governance must actually deliver. And it points us toward an instrument I have not yet mentioned — executive compensation. Because incentives, ultimately, dictate behaviour far more reliably than mission statements do. Consider how the typical pay package is structured around short-horizon share-price targets. You can lecture a chief executive about long-term stakeholder value all you like, but if her bonus vests on next quarter's earnings, the quarter will win. Every time.

There is a striking empirical thread here. Research associated with Lucian Bebchuk at Harvard documents how share buybacks have, in many firms, become a mechanism for inflating per-share metrics and, conveniently, executive payouts — capital that might otherwise have funded wages, research or decarbonisation. [pause] So the ESG report can glow on the cover page while the capital-allocation decisions underneath tell the opposite story.

This is the gap between disclosure and substance, and it is why, um, transparency alone is necessary but nowhere near sufficient. You can mandate reporting and still get theatre. Which raises the decisive question for the policy discussion ahead — whether accountability can be engineered through incentive design rather than merely demanded through rhetoric, and if so…

> The synthesis is overdue: stakeholder theory needs robust governance, and governance needs harmonised, audit-grade ESG metrics. Without all three pillars, the edifice collapses. Now, please consult table three…

blocks.text: (e) Bài mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~172 từ)
The diagram delineates the eight-stage ESG audit pipeline by which a multinational conglomerate is independently assessed prior to publishing its annual sustainability report.

Overall, the procedure is largely sequential yet contains one critical feedback loop, and only a single stage is outsourced to an external party - features which arguably reveal both the strengths and the limitations of the prevailing corporate governance framework.

The pipeline is initiated when the board issues a formal audit mandate. Subsequently, a stakeholder consultation is conducted with employees, NGOs and institutional investors, after which raw data on emissions, labour practices and supply chains are collated. These figures are then benchmarked against industry-standard ESG metrics; should performance prove substandard, the process reverts to the data-collection stage for remediation.

Once the benchmarks are met, an independent third party verifies the findings, and a comprehensive audit trail is documented and digitally timestamped. Finally, the board reviews the dossier under its fiduciary duty before authorising public disclosure, thereby ensuring that the report eventually released is both materially accurate and legally defensible.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~191 từ)

The flow chart delineates the eight discrete stages through which a multinational conglomerate is independently audited on environmental, social and governance criteria before its annual sustainability report reaches the public.

Overall, what is most striking is that the procedure, though predominantly linear, is punctuated by a single corrective feedback loop, and that verification alone is entrusted to an external party - an arrangement that arguably exposes the tension between internal control and genuine independence.

The sequence is set in motion once the board commissions a formal mandate. Thereafter, affected stakeholders are consulted, and granular data spanning carbon emissions, labour conditions and supply chains are systematically collated. These figures are subsequently measured against peer benchmarks; where performance is found wanting, the pipeline cycles back to data collection, so that no deficient metric advances unremedied.

Only when these thresholds are satisfied does an independent assessor verify the dossier, whereupon an immutable, timestamped audit trail is logged and salient risks are flagged. The penultimate stage sees directors scrutinise the record under their fiduciary duty, and it is only with their sanction that the validated report is finally disclosed to regulators and the market alike.

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~279 words)

Whether corporations exist solely to enrich their shareholders is one of the most contested questions in modern business ethics. While some commentators continue to defend shareholder primacy, I largely disagree with the view, because corporations operate within wider social and ecological systems whose health ultimately determines their own.

Supporters of the traditional model argue that a clear focus on returns disciplines management. It is the pressure to deliver quarterly results that, in their view, prevents executives from squandering funds on vanity projects. Moreover, profitable firms generate jobs, fund pensions and contribute taxes, all of which arguably benefit society far more than performative philanthropy. From this angle, prioritising shareholders is not selfish but efficient, since a thriving business is the precondition for almost every other social good a company might deliver.

However, this position increasingly seems out of step with how value is actually created today. Modern companies rely on stakeholders far beyond their investors - workers, suppliers, regulators and the communities hosting their factories. When firms cut corners to flatter the bottom line, the costs do not disappear; they are simply transferred to society as pollution, sweatshops or unsafe products. The 2008 financial crisis showed how the single-minded pursuit of returns can destroy the very economy on which those returns depend. The rise of ESG investing further suggests that even shareholders themselves now demand a broader scorecard.

In conclusion, I disagree strongly with the proposition that shareholder value should override everything else. A more balanced model, often described as stakeholder capitalism, would better protect long-term profitability while limiting social harm. What the corporate world needs is not a softer version of greed, but a genuinely broader definition of success.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~295 words)

Few doctrines have shaped contemporary capitalism as profoundly as Milton Friedman's claim that the social responsibility of business is to increase its profits. While the slogan retains rhetorical force, I disagree strongly with the proposition that shareholder value should override every other consideration, for it rests on an outdated reading of where corporate value actually originates.

Defenders of shareholder primacy do raise legitimate points. By anchoring management to a single, measurable objective, the doctrine arguably reduces agency costs and curbs executive self-dealing. Profitable corporations, in turn, finance pensions, generate tax revenue and discipline inefficient competitors out of the market. It is precisely this hard-edged accountability, proponents contend, that distinguishes private enterprise from politically captured state monopolies.

Yet this account understates the breadth of fiduciary duty in the twenty-first century. Modern firms depend on stakeholders whose contributions appear nowhere on the balance sheet: workers absorbing precarity, regulators granting licences and ecosystems supplying inputs. What shareholder maximisation has tended to produce, particularly in resource-intensive sectors, is a systematic transfer of risk onto these groups - wage suppression, sweatshop subcontracting and environmental externalities masked as efficiency. Were such costs internalised, many headline returns would evaporate overnight. Nowhere is this clearer than in the post-2008 banking sector, where shareholder-driven risk-taking demanded taxpayer bailouts worth trillions.

Furthermore, the trajectory of capital markets is itself shifting. The rapid mainstreaming of ESG criteria suggests that long-term investors increasingly penalise narrow profit-maximisation, while reputational shocks now translate swiftly into lost market value. What sustainable companies appear to grasp is that legitimacy, not merely earnings, secures the social licence to operate. On balance, then, shareholder value remains a useful metric, but elevating it above all else is intellectually obsolete and commercially imprudent; stakeholder capitalism, properly governed, is the more defensible model for our age.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 dùng cấu trúc phức cao cấp xuyên suốt (inversion 'Nowhere is this clearer than...', đảo ngữ điều kiện 'Were such costs internalised...', cleft 'What sustainable companies appear to grasp is...') trong khi Band 7 chỉ dùng một vài lần.

•  Band 8 dẫn bằng chứng cụ thể và sắc hơn ('bailouts worth trillions', 'resource-intensive sectors') cùng nominalisation dày đặc ('wage suppression', 'social licence to operate', 'profit-maximisation'), nâng Task Response và Lexical Resource.
•  Band 8 có register học thuật nhất quán và cohesion tinh tế ('for it rests on...', 'in turn', 'On balance, then'), loại bỏ cụm đời thường như 'a softer version of greed' của bản 7.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Philanthropy' là hoạt động từ thiện, thể hiện qua các khoản quyên góp hào phóng vì phúc lợi của người khác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> While many wealthy CEOs engage in genuine **philanthropy** to support community development, others are widely accused of greenwashing.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Phil-' nghĩa là yêu mến, '-anthropy' liên quan đến con người, ghép lại thành 'yêu mến con người' tức là hoạt động từ thiện.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'philanthropy' (danh từ trừu tượng, chỉ hoạt động) với 'philanthropist' (danh từ chỉ người thực hiện hoạt động đó).
vocabulary.definition_en: The practice of donating money, time, or resources to promote the welfare of others, especially through generous charitable giving.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Hoạt động từ thiện, làm việc thiện nguyện vì phúc lợi cộng đồng.
vocabulary.example: While many wealthy CEOs engage in genuine philanthropy to support community development, others are widely accused of greenwashing.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Phil-' (yêu mến) + '-anthropy' (con người) → 'yêu mến con người' → hoạt động từ thiện.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Monopoly' chỉ tình trạng một công ty duy nhất kiểm soát hoàn toàn một thị trường hoặc ngành hàng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The government is investigating the giant tech company for **monopolistic** behaviour.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Mono' nghĩa là 'một', nên 'monopoly' là khi chỉ một doanh nghiệp duy nhất thống trị cả thị trường.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Monopoly' đi với giới từ 'on/of' (a monopoly on/of something), không phải 'monopoly for'.
vocabulary.definition_en: The exclusive possession or control of the supply of, or trade in, a commodity or service in a particular market.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Sự độc quyền, quyền kiểm soát duy nhất đối với một thị trường hoặc sản phẩm.
vocabulary.example: The government is investigating the giant tech company for monopolistic behaviour.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Mono-' nghĩa là 'một' → chỉ một công ty nắm toàn bộ thị trường.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Transparency' là sự minh bạch, cởi mở và dễ kiểm chứng, đặc biệt trong hoạt động kinh doanh.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Consumers now demand total **transparency** regarding how their products are manufactured.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Trans-' là xuyên qua, '-parent' là hiện rõ, ghép lại là nhìn xuyên thấu mọi thứ, tức là minh bạch.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Transparency' (danh từ trừu tượng) khác với 'transparent' (tính từ); học viên hay viết sai 'the company's transparent' thay vì 'the company's transparency'.
vocabulary.definition_en: The quality of being open, honest, and easy to perceive or verify, especially regarding business practices and information.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Sự minh bạch, tính công khai rõ ràng trong hoạt động hoặc thông tin.
vocabulary.example: Consumers now demand total transparency regarding how their products are manufactured.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Trans-' (xuyên qua) + '-parent' (hiện rõ) → nhìn xuyên thấu, rõ ràng, minh bạch.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Stakeholders' là những cá nhân hoặc nhóm có lợi ích liên quan đến một doanh nghiệp, không chỉ riêng cổ đông.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> They must always consider the broader social impact on all **stakeholders**, not just their shareholders.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Stake' là phần lợi ích, 'holder' là người nắm giữ, nên 'stakeholder' là người có lợi ích liên quan trong công ty.
vocabulary.common_error: Phân biệt 'stakeholders' (mọi bên liên quan: nhân viên, khách hàng, cộng đồng...) với 'shareholders' (chỉ cổ đông sở hữu cổ phần) — hai từ dễ nhầm do gần âm.
vocabulary.definition_en: Persons or groups with an interest, share, or concern in a business or organisation, such as employees, customers, and investors.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Các bên liên quan có lợi ích hoặc mối quan tâm đối với một doanh nghiệp.
vocabulary.example: They must always consider the broader social impact on all stakeholders, not just their shareholders.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Stake' (cổ phần/lợi ích) + 'holder' (người giữ) → người giữ lợi ích trong công ty.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Merger' là sự kiện hai công ty sáp nhập lại thành một thực thể duy nhất.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The two rival firms announced their **merger** to the press yesterday.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình dung 'merge' như hai làn xe nhập một trên cao tốc, tương tự hai công ty hợp nhất thành một qua một 'merger'.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Merger' là danh từ, động từ tương ứng là 'merge' (không phải 'merger' dùng như động từ).
vocabulary.definition_en: The combining of two or more companies into a single one, often undertaken to gain market share or efficiency.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Sự sáp nhập giữa hai hoặc nhiều công ty thành một.
vocabulary.example: The two rival firms announced their merger to the press yesterday.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Liên tưởng 'merge' như hai làn xe nhập làm một trên cao tốc → hai công ty 'nhập làn' thành một.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Greenwashing' là việc giả vờ thân thiện với môi trường nhằm mục đích tiếp thị, trong khi thực chất không phải vậy.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Others are widely accused of **greenwashing**, merely pretending to be eco-friendly to boost sales.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Green' là màu xanh môi trường, 'washing' là tẩy rửa/đánh bóng, ghép lại là 'tẩy xanh' hình ảnh một cách giả dối.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Greenwashing' luôn mang nghĩa tiêu cực (lừa dối); không nên dùng để mô tả nỗ lực môi trường thật sự, dù nhỏ.
vocabulary.definition_en: The deceptive practice of marketing products, policies, or a company's image as environmentally friendly when they are not.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Hành vi 'tẩy xanh' — giả vờ thân thiện với môi trường để đánh bóng hình ảnh, đánh lừa người tiêu dùng.
vocabulary.example: Others are widely accused of greenwashing, merely pretending to be eco-friendly to boost sales.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Green' (xanh, môi trường) + 'washing' (tẩy rửa/đánh bóng) → tẩy xanh hình ảnh giả tạo.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Conglomerate' là một tập đoàn lớn được hình thành từ việc sáp nhập nhiều công ty hoạt động trong các lĩnh vực khác nhau.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The company I'd like to talk about is Vinamilk, which has since transformed into a publicly listed **conglomerate** with a market capitalisation exceeding 150 trillion VND.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Giống như đá conglomerate trong địa chất là nhiều mảnh đá nhỏ kết dính thành một khối, một 'conglomerate' kinh doanh là nhiều công ty nhỏ hợp thành một tập đoàn lớn.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Conglomerate' nhấn mạnh tính đa dạng ngành nghề, khác với 'monopoly' (độc quyền một ngành) — hai khái niệm không đồng nghĩa.
vocabulary.definition_en: A large corporation formed by the merging of several distinct and diverse firms, often operating across unrelated industries.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Tập đoàn lớn hình thành từ việc sáp nhập nhiều công ty khác nhau, hoạt động đa ngành.
vocabulary.example: The company I'd like to talk about is Vinamilk, which has since transformed into a publicly listed conglomerate with a market capitalisation exceeding 150 trillion VND.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Liên tưởng đá conglomerate (đá cuội kết) trong địa chất — nhiều loại đá nhỏ 'kết dính' thành một khối, giống nhiều công ty nhỏ hợp thành một tập đoàn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Niche' là một phân khúc thị trường nhỏ, chuyên biệt, dành riêng cho một loại sản phẩm hoặc khách hàng nhất định.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Small startups, eager to avoid the excessive red tape of large corporations, often succeed by targeting a specific **niche** market.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hãy hình dung 'niche' như một khe hở nhỏ trên tường mà chỉ vừa khít một món đồ đặc biệt, giống như một phân khúc thị trường chuyên biệt.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Niche' có thể vừa là danh từ vừa là tính từ ('a niche' / 'a niche product'); không thêm 's' khi dùng như tính từ.
vocabulary.definition_en: A specialised, narrow segment of a market for which a specific product or service is designed.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Thị trường ngách, phân khúc nhỏ và chuyên biệt.
vocabulary.example: Small startups, eager to avoid the excessive red tape of large corporations, often succeed by targeting a specific niche market.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung một 'khe hở nhỏ' (niche gốc nghĩa là hốc tường) trên thị trường mà chỉ sản phẩm chuyên biệt mới lấp đầy được.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Accountability' là trách nhiệm giải trình, tức là nghĩa vụ phải chịu trách nhiệm và giải thích rõ ràng cho hành động của mình.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Greater transparency and **accountability** are pivotal to rebuilding public trust in corporations.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Account' nghĩa là giải trình, thêm '-ability' thành khả năng phải giải trình, tức là 'accountability'.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Accountability' (trách nhiệm giải trình trước người khác) khác với 'responsibility' (trách nhiệm nói chung) — accountability nhấn mạnh việc phải 'giải trình' khi có sai sót.
vocabulary.definition_en: The state of being responsible for one's actions and required to explain or justify them to others.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Trách nhiệm giải trình, nghĩa vụ phải chịu trách nhiệm và giải thích hành động của mình.
vocabulary.example: Greater transparency and accountability are pivotal to rebuilding public trust in corporations.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Account' (giải trình/tường trình) + '-ability' (khả năng) → khả năng phải giải trình cho hành động của mình.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Malpractice' là hành vi sai phạm hoặc tắc trách trong nghề nghiệp, đặc biệt liên quan đến đạo đức kinh doanh.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The company faced severe allegations of unethical practices, and campaigners called for an investigation into corporate **malpractice**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Mal-' nghĩa là xấu/sai, ghép với 'practice' (hành nghề) thành 'malpractice' — hành nghề sai trái.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Malpractice' là danh từ không đếm được khi chỉ khái niệm chung (widespread malpractice); chỉ đếm được khi nói 'a case/instance of malpractice'.
vocabulary.definition_en: Improper, negligent, or unethical professional conduct, especially by a business, official, or practitioner.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Sai phạm nghề nghiệp/đạo đức, hành vi thiếu chuẩn mực hoặc tắc trách trong công việc.
vocabulary.example: The company faced severe allegations of unethical practices, and campaigners called for an investigation into corporate malpractice.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Mal-' (xấu/sai) + 'practice' (thực hành/hành nghề) → hành nghề sai trái.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Sustainable' nghĩa là bền vững, có thể duy trì lâu dài mà không làm cạn kiệt tài nguyên hay gây hại.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Embedding **sustainability** into core operations is no longer optional but a commercial imperative.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Sus-' liên quan đến giữ, 'tain' là nắm giữ, ghép lại là giữ vững lâu dài — chính là ý nghĩa của 'sustainable'.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Sustainable' (tính từ) khác với 'sustainability' (danh từ trừu tượng); học viên hay viết 'the sustainable of the company' thay vì 'the sustainability of the company'.
vocabulary.definition_en: Able to be maintained at a certain level over the long term without depleting resources or causing lasting harm.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Bền vững, có thể duy trì lâu dài mà không gây cạn kiệt tài nguyên hay tác hại lâu dài.
vocabulary.example: Embedding sustainability into core operations is no longer optional but a commercial imperative.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Sus-' (dưới/duy trì) + 'tain' (giữ) → giữ vững được lâu dài, tức là bền vững.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Exploitation' là hành vi bóc lột, lợi dụng người khác một cách bất công để trục lợi, thường gặp trong bối cảnh lao động.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Labour **exploitation** within global supply chains has come under intense public scrutiny.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Liên tưởng 'exploit' (khai thác) bị đẩy đến mức cực đoan, khai thác cả sức lao động con người, trở thành 'exploitation' — bóc lột.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Exploitation' (bóc lột, nghĩa xấu) khác với 'exploration' (khám phá) — hai từ dễ nhầm do gần âm nhưng nghĩa hoàn toàn khác nhau.
vocabulary.definition_en: The action of treating someone unfairly in order to benefit from their work, especially by paying them too little or overworking them.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Sự bóc lột, hành vi lợi dụng người khác một cách bất công để trục lợi.
vocabulary.example: Labour exploitation within global supply chains has come under intense public scrutiny.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Exploit' vốn có thể mang nghĩa trung tính (khai thác), nhưng 'exploitation' trong kinh doanh thường mang nghĩa tiêu cực — khai thác con người quá mức.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Divest nghĩa là thoái vốn, bán bớt tài sản hoặc khoản đầu tư, thường vì lý do chiến lược hoặc đạo đức.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Under pressure from shareholders, the fund decided to **divest** from companies with poor environmental records.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Di-' nghĩa là tách ra, 'vest' liên quan đến việc khoác vào, nên 'divest' là hành động 'cởi bỏ' khoản đầu tư, tức bán đi.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'divest' (thoái vốn, bán đi) với 'invest' (đầu tư, bỏ vốn vào) — hai từ trái nghĩa dễ gây nhầm lẫn khi nghe nhanh.
vocabulary.definition_en: To sell off a business, investment, or asset, often for financial, strategic, or ethical reasons.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Thoái vốn, bán bớt tài sản/khoản đầu tư (thường vì lý do chiến lược hoặc đạo đức)
vocabulary.example: Under pressure from shareholders, the fund decided to divest from companies with poor environmental records.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Di-' (tách ra) + 'vest' (gốc Latin liên quan đến 'trang bị/khoác vào') → 'divest' là 'cởi bỏ' khoản đầu tư, tức bán đi.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Whistleblower nghĩa là người tố giác, người tiết lộ hành vi sai trái xảy ra bên trong một tổ chức.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A **whistleblower** exposed the company's fraudulent accounting practices to financial regulators.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình dung một trọng tài thổi còi để dừng trận đấu khi phát hiện phạm luật — 'whistleblower' cũng 'thổi còi' báo động sai phạm trong công ty.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Whistleblower' viết liền hoặc có gạch nối tùy phong cách, nhưng không viết tách rời thành ba từ 'whistle blow er'.
vocabulary.definition_en: A person who reports illegal or unethical activity within an organisation, typically to authorities or the public.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Người tố giác, người tiết lộ hành vi sai trái trong một tổ chức
vocabulary.example: A whistleblower exposed the company's fraudulent accounting practices to financial regulators.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung một trọng tài thổi còi (blow the whistle) để dừng trận đấu khi phát hiện phạm luật — 'whistleblower' cũng 'thổi còi' báo động sai phạm.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'At the expense of' nghĩa là phải đánh đổi hoặc gây thiệt hại cho một bên khác để đạt được lợi ích.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Shareholder returns should not be prioritised **at the expense of** broader stakeholder welfare.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hãy hình dung một chiếc cân: bên này được lợi thì bên kia phải trả giá — đó chính là ý nghĩa của 'at the expense of'.
collocations: at the expense of the environment
growth at the expense of quality
vocabulary.common_error: Không nhầm 'at the expense of' (nghĩa ẩn dụ: đánh đổi/thiệt hại) với nghĩa đen 'chi phí' của từ 'expense' trong kế toán.
vocabulary.definition_en: In a way that causes harm to someone or something else, or sacrifices one thing in order to gain another.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Với cái giá phải trả là..., đánh đổi/hy sinh một thứ khác để đạt được điều gì đó.
vocabulary.example: Shareholder returns should not be prioritised at the expense of broader stakeholder welfare.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung một chiếc cân: bên này được lợi, bên kia phải trả giá ('expense') — đó là bản chất của 'at the expense of'.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'A pressing concern' là một mối lo ngại cấp bách, cần được giải quyết ngay lập tức.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Ensuring supply-chain transparency has become **a pressing concern** for multinational conglomerates.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Pressing' giống như một áp lực đang đè nén, buộc vấn đề phải được xử lý ngay — đó là 'a pressing concern'.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Pressing' ở đây là tính từ nghĩa 'cấp bách', không liên quan đến nghĩa đen 'ấn/nhấn' của động từ 'press'.
vocabulary.definition_en: An issue that urgently requires attention or action because of its seriousness or urgency.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Mối lo ngại cấp bách, vấn đề cần được giải quyết ngay.
vocabulary.example: Ensuring supply-chain transparency has become a pressing concern for multinational conglomerates.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Pressing' như một áp lực đang 'đè nén' ('press') buộc phải giải quyết ngay — một mối lo cấp bách.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Cut corners' nghĩa là làm việc một cách sơ sài, cắt giảm chất lượng hoặc an toàn để tiết kiệm chi phí hay thời gian.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> They did a bad job and **cut corners** on safety regulations in order to save money.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hãy hình dung một người đi tắt qua góc phòng thay vì đi đường vòng đầy đủ — đó chính là hình ảnh của 'cut corners'.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Cut corners' luôn ở dạng số nhiều 'corners', không dùng 'cut a corner' hay 'cut corner'.
vocabulary.definition_en: To do something in the easiest or cheapest way, often by ignoring rules or sacrificing quality and safety.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Làm ẩu, cắt giảm chất lượng/an toàn để tiết kiệm chi phí hoặc thời gian.
vocabulary.example: They did a bad job and cut corners on safety regulations in order to save money.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung người đi tắt qua góc phòng thay vì đi đường vòng đầy đủ — 'cắt góc' để nhanh và rẻ hơn, nhưng kém an toàn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Cut-throat' mô tả một môi trường cạnh tranh cực kỳ khốc liệt, nơi các đối thủ không khoan nhượng với nhau.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> It is a very **cut-throat** market where everyone fights hard to win, and small businesses often find it incredibly hard to survive.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình ảnh 'cắt cổ' rùng rợn của cụm từ này tượng trưng cho một môi trường cạnh tranh không khoan nhượng.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Cut-throat' là tính từ ghép luôn có gạch nối, không viết rời thành 'cut throat' khi dùng để mô tả cạnh tranh khốc liệt.
vocabulary.definition_en: Fiercely competitive and ruthless, with little regard for ethics in the pursuit of success.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Cạnh tranh khốc liệt, không khoan nhượng.
vocabulary.example: It is a very cut-throat market where everyone fights hard to win, and small businesses often find it incredibly hard to survive.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình ảnh 'cắt cổ' (cut throat) rùng rợn tượng trưng cho một môi trường cạnh tranh không khoan nhượng, sẵn sàng 'triệt hạ' đối thủ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Go bust' là thành ngữ thân mật chỉ việc một công ty phá sản và buộc phải đóng cửa.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Following the economic crash, hundreds of local retail shops **went bust** and had to close down entirely.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Bust' nghĩa là vỡ tan hoàn toàn, nên khi một công ty 'go bust' nghĩa là nó đã 'vỡ' về tài chính và phải đóng cửa.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Go bust' là thành ngữ thân mật (informal), trong văn viết học thuật nên dùng 'go bankrupt' hoặc 'declare bankruptcy' thay thế.
vocabulary.definition_en: To become bankrupt and be forced to close down, usually because of financial failure.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Phá sản, phải đóng cửa vì thất bại tài chính.
vocabulary.example: Following the economic crash, hundreds of local retail shops went bust and had to close down entirely.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Bust' nghĩa là vỡ tan/hỏng hoàn toàn — công ty 'go bust' là 'vỡ' tài chính, phải đóng cửa.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'In the black' là thành ngữ chỉ tình trạng công ty đang có lãi, tài chính lành mạnh.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> After a difficult first quarter, the company is finally operating **in the black** again and making a profit.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Sổ sách kế toán xưa ghi lãi bằng mực đen và lỗ bằng mực đỏ, nên 'in the black' nghĩa là công ty đang có lãi.
vocabulary.common_error: Đối lập trực tiếp với 'in the red' (thua lỗ) — hai thành ngữ bắt nguồn từ màu mực ghi sổ kế toán truyền thống (đen = lãi, đỏ = lỗ).
vocabulary.definition_en: In a state of financial profit or solvency, rather than debt.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Có lãi, ở trạng thái tài chính lành mạnh (trái với thua lỗ).
vocabulary.example: After a difficult first quarter, the company is finally operating in the black again and making a profit.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Sổ sách kế toán xưa ghi lãi bằng mực đen, lỗ bằng mực đỏ — 'in the black' nghĩa là đang có lãi.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Above board' nghĩa là hoàn toàn hợp pháp và minh bạch, không có điều gì bị che giấu.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> We must ensure that all our business transactions are strictly **above board** and legal.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Thành ngữ này xuất phát từ việc đánh bài: giữ tay bài ở trên bàn để mọi người nhìn thấy rõ, không gian lận.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Above board' là cụm tính từ vị ngữ (sau động từ 'be'), không dùng trực tiếp trước danh từ như 'an above-board deal' (dù cách này thỉnh thoảng vẫn gặp có gạch nối).
vocabulary.definition_en: Completely legal, honest, and open, with nothing hidden or improper.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Hoàn toàn hợp pháp, minh bạch, không có gì che giấu.
vocabulary.example: We must ensure that all our business transactions are strictly above board and legal.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Xuất xứ từ đánh bài: giữ tay bài 'trên bàn' (above board/table) để mọi người thấy rõ, không gian lận.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Red tape' là thủ tục hành chính, quan liêu rườm rà gây cản trở cho doanh nghiệp.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The new strict regulation creates far too much **red tape** for young entrepreneurs trying to start a company.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Thành ngữ bắt nguồn từ dây ruy băng đỏ buộc hồ sơ chính thức thời xưa — càng nhiều dây đỏ càng nhiều thủ tục rườm rà.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Red tape' luôn không đếm được (uncountable): không nói 'a red tape' hay 'red tapes'.
vocabulary.definition_en: Excessive bureaucracy or official rules and procedures that cause unnecessary delay in getting something done.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Thủ tục hành chính rườm rà, quan liêu gây cản trở.
vocabulary.example: The new strict regulation creates far too much red tape for young entrepreneurs trying to start a company.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Xuất xứ từ dây ruy băng đỏ dùng buộc hồ sơ chính thức thời xưa — càng nhiều dây đỏ, càng nhiều thủ tục rườm rà.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Corner the market' nghĩa là giành quyền kiểm soát, thống lĩnh thị trường của một sản phẩm hoặc dịch vụ cụ thể.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> They managed to **corner the market** on electric scooters by offering the lowest prices.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hãy hình dung việc dồn toàn bộ thị trường vào một góc mà chỉ một công ty duy nhất kiểm soát được — đó là 'corner the market'.
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm này dùng giới từ 'on' hoặc 'in' trước sản phẩm ('corner the market on/in electric scooters'), không dùng 'for'.
vocabulary.definition_en: To gain control of the supply of a particular product or service, dominating that market segment.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Thống lĩnh/độc chiếm thị trường của một sản phẩm hoặc dịch vụ cụ thể.
vocabulary.example: They managed to corner the market on electric scooters by offering the lowest prices.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung 'dồn' toàn bộ thị trường vào một góc ('corner') mà chỉ một công ty kiểm soát được.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
'Fiduciary duty' là nghĩa vụ ủy thác, tức trách nhiệm pháp lý phải hành động vì lợi ích tài chính của người khác, thường áp dụng cho giám đốc công ty.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Directors scrutinise the dossier, bearing legal responsibility under their **fiduciary duty** for the accuracy of the disclosed report.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Fiduciary' bắt nguồn từ tiếng Latin 'fides' nghĩa là niềm tin, nên 'fiduciary duty' là nghĩa vụ dựa trên sự tín thác tuyệt đối.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Fiduciary' hay bị phát âm/viết nhầm; trọng âm rơi vào âm tiết thứ hai (fi-DU-cia-ry), không phải âm tiết đầu.
vocabulary.definition_en: A legal or ethical obligation of one party (such as a company director) to act solely in the financial interests of another party.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Nghĩa vụ ủy thác — trách nhiệm pháp lý phải hành động vì lợi ích tài chính của bên khác.
vocabulary.example: Directors scrutinise the dossier, bearing legal responsibility under their fiduciary duty for the accuracy of the disclosed report.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Fiduciary' bắt nguồn từ tiếng Latin 'fides' (niềm tin) — nghĩa vụ dựa trên sự tín thác, phải trung thành tuyệt đối vì lợi ích người khác.
